prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and practically relevant problem: extracting product attributes in a genuinely open-world, lightly supervised setting, where the system must both expand known attribute types and discover previously unseen ones without explicit type descriptions at inference time. That setting is well motivated for e-commerce, where attribute vocabularies evolve quickly and exhaustive annotation is expensive. The paper’s main contributions are a new dataset, WoaM, and a method, Amacer, that combines syntax-based candidate generation, supervised contrastive learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for known types, and two forms of weak regularization aimed at unseen attribute discovery. Overall, I found the paper interesting and reasonably strong empirically, with a clear practical motivation and several thoughtful design choices. At the same time, there are some methodological and evaluation issues that limit how conclusively the results support the broader claims.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the task formulation. The distinction from prior closed-world extraction and zero-shot extraction is meaningful: here the model is not told which new types to look for, and must instead induce useful clusters from weak supervision. That is a realistic and underexplored setting. The dataset also appears to be a valuable contribution. In particular, including both titles and bullet points is a good design choice, since bullet points are richer and more realistic than titles alone, and the statistics showing substantially more unseen types and values there support the claim that this is a harder and more realistic benchmark than prior title-only settings. The hybrid seed construction process is also sensible from an applied perspective: bootstrap from existing retailer metadata, aggressively sanitize, then lightly curate. This is a plausible workflow for industrial deployment.

The proposed method is also fairly coherent. The syntax-based candidate generation is simple but well justified. It avoids over-reliance on seed supervision and seems better suited than segmentation for longer bullet-point text. The supervised contrastive objective over seed values is standard but appropriate, and the adaptive expansion stage is a nice practical mechanism for assigning candidates to known seed types before clustering the remainder. The most novel part is the use of implicit signals for unseen attributes: the bullet-point co-occurrence heuristic and the latent-attribute regularizer. These are intuitive ways to inject structure beyond the seed set, and the ablations suggest they help, especially on new types.

Empirically, the gains are substantial on the proposed benchmark. The reported improvements over OA-Mine and tagging baselines are large enough to be meaningful, and the decomposition by seed/new types and title/bullet-point subsets is useful. I especially appreciated the “gold spans as candidates” analysis, which helps separate candidate generation from representation learning and grouping. The qualitative examples are also informative: they show both successful vocabulary expansion and the characteristic failure mode of mapping unseen types into semantically nearby seen ones.

That said, I have several concerns.

First, the evaluation protocol is somewhat hard to interpret, especially the main “pseudo-F1” metric. The paper averages Jaccard, ARI, and NMI and treats that average as a kind of precision, then combines it with recall into an F1-like score. This is unconventional and not obviously well founded. Jaccard, ARI, and NMI are clustering agreement metrics with different scales and behaviors; averaging them and calling the result “pseudo precision” is heuristic at best. Because the paper emphasizes the final F1 as the main metric and bases many claims on it, this weakens the rigor of the evaluation. I would strongly prefer reporting the underlying metrics separately as primary results, or using a more standard clustering evaluation framework. At minimum, the paper should justify why this aggregation is meaningful and robust, and ideally show that conclusions are unchanged under alternative summaries.

Second, the comparison to baselines is not entirely clean. Several baselines differ from Amacer in more than one component at once, especially candidate generation. The paper does include OA-Mine* and Amacer* variants to partially control for this, which is good, but the overall narrative still mixes gains from candidate generation, representation learning, and grouping. Since candidate generation appears to be a major driver of performance, it would be helpful to isolate its contribution more systematically. For example, how much of the final gain over OA-Mine comes from syntax-based candidates alone versus the new regularization versus adaptive expansion? The current ablations point in this direction but do not fully disentangle the components.

Third, the novelty of some modeling pieces is moderate. Supervised contrastive learning over seed values, adaptive thresholding based on support-set cohesion, and DBSCAN over residual candidates are sensible engineering choices, but not individually very novel. The main novelty lies in the latent-attribute regularization and perhaps the bullet-point self-supervision heuristic. Even there, the latent-variable formulation is closely adapted from neural topic modeling. This is not necessarily a problem if the empirical contribution is strong, but it means the paper should be careful not to overstate methodological novelty. In its current form, the paper sometimes presents combinations of known ideas as more novel than they are.

Fourth, the latent-attribute component is interesting but under-analyzed. The paper acknowledges topic collapse qualitatively, but does not quantify how severe it is or how sensitive performance is to the number of latent attributes K. Since this component is claimed to contribute most of the regularization gain, I would like to see stronger evidence that it is learning meaningful structure rather than acting as a generic auxiliary objective. For instance, sensitivity to K, diversity metrics over latent attributes, or comparisons to simpler unsupervised regularizers would strengthen the claim. Similarly, the self-supervised bullet-point heuristic assumes different bullet points within a product discuss different aspects, which is plausible but noisy; some empirical validation of that assumption would help.

Fifth, the dataset construction raises some questions about bias and scope. The benchmark covers only four categories, all from Amazon, and only English text. That is acceptable for an initial study, but it limits the generality of the conclusions. More importantly, the seed set is derived from retailer-provided attributes and then curated. This may bias the benchmark toward attributes that are already salient in retailer metadata, even if the test set includes unseen types. It would be useful to know more about inter-annotator agreement on the test set, especially because the notion of a “reasonable attribute value” in an open-world setting is subjective. The paper mentions two annotators but does not report agreement statistics in the provided text. Given that span boundaries and type granularity are central to the task, agreement is important.

Sixth, the candidate generation stage, while effective, may be more brittle than the paper suggests. It depends on POS tagging quality and on POS patterns extracted from profile attributes. This could work well in English product text with relatively formulaic phrasing, but may degrade in noisier domains or languages with weaker tagging tools. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but I think it is more central than presented, because candidate generation is foundational and the span extraction scores remain fairly low. In fact, Table 5 suggests that span extraction is still a major bottleneck. This means some of the clustering improvements may be contingent on a candidate set whose quality is not yet strong enough for broader deployment.

I also have a few smaller technical questions. The supervised contrastive loss denominator appears to sum over negatives only, whereas standard supervised contrastive formulations usually normalize over all non-anchor examples including positives; perhaps this is just notation, but it should be clarified. The adaptive threshold in Eq. 2 uses average pairwise cosine distance within the support set; intuitively, more coherent seed sets should have smaller distances, so multiplying by delta gives a smaller threshold. That makes sense, but the paper should discuss what happens for heterogeneous attributes whose seed values are semantically broad. Also, because each span is forced to a single type and overlaps are disallowed, some naturally multi-faceted values may be mishandled; this is understandable for evaluation simplicity, but worth discussing as a task limitation.

In terms of writing and presentation, the paper is generally understandable, but there are many grammatical issues and awkward phrasings throughout. These do not obscure the main ideas, but they do reduce polish. Some terminology could also be tightened. For example, “pseudo precision” is potentially misleading, and “discovering values from 39% unseen attribute types” should be stated more precisely. The paper would benefit from a careful proofreading pass and some simplification of claims.

My overall assessment is positive. The paper addresses a meaningful problem, introduces a useful benchmark, and presents a practical method that appears to outperform relevant baselines by a substantial margin. The work is especially valuable as a step toward more realistic open-world information extraction in e-commerce. However, the evaluation methodology is somewhat ad hoc, the novelty is more in the task and system combination than in any single modeling idea, and some important analyses are missing, particularly around annotation quality, sensitivity, and the latent-attribute component.

I would recommend acceptance if the venue values practical task-setting advances and benchmark contributions, but with some reservations. To strengthen the paper, I would encourage the authors to: provide stronger justification or alternatives for the main evaluation metric; report annotation agreement and more dataset details; add sensitivity analyses for K and other key hyperparameters; better disentangle gains from candidate generation versus representation learning; and moderate novelty claims around the modeling components. With these improvements, the paper would be significantly stronger.

My main strengths are the practical and well-motivated task formulation, the useful new dataset with richer product text, the coherent weakly supervised pipeline, and the strong empirical gains including on unseen attribute types. My main weaknesses are the unconventional main metric, incomplete disentanglement of component contributions, limited analysis of the latent-attribute regularizer, and questions about generality and annotation subjectivity.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting for e-commerce, where the goal is both to expand values for known seed attribute types and to discover entirely new attribute types without explicit type descriptions. To support this setting, the authors construct the WoaM dataset across four Amazon product categories with curated seed attributes and human-annotated test data. They propose Amacer, a pipeline consisting of syntax-based candidate span generation, supervised contrastive representation learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for known attributes, DBSCAN clustering for remaining candidates, and two additional regularizers for new attribute discovery: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence contrastive loss and an unsupervised latent-attribute topic-model-like objective. Experiments show consistent gains over closed-world tagging baselines and OA-Mine variants, with the strongest improvements attributed to better candidate generation, supervised contrastive learning, and the proposed regularization for unseen attributes.
strengths: The paper addresses a practically meaningful and underexplored task setting: open-world attribute mining under limited supervision, which is more realistic than closed-world extraction or zero-shot extraction with predefined target types.

The dataset contribution appears valuable: WoaM includes titles and bullet points, multiple categories, curated seed sets, and explicit evaluation of unseen attribute types, which fills a gap in prior benchmarks focused on titles or noisier distant supervision.
The proposed system is modular and intuitively motivated, combining candidate generation, representation learning, and clustering in a coherent pipeline.
Empirical results are strong relative to the chosen baselines, with Amacer outperforming OA-Mine and tagging approaches by substantial margins on the paper's main pseudo-F1 metric.

The ablation comparisons are reasonably informative: syntax-based candidates outperform segmentation, adaptive expansion improves recall, and the regularization terms help especially on new attribute types.
The paper is generally well written and clearly explains the task motivation, dataset construction process, and the role of each modeling component.
The qualitative examples help illustrate both successful seed expansion and the difficulty of discovering genuinely new attribute types.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is unconventional and somewhat problematic: the main metric defines 'pseudo precision' as the average of Jaccard, ARI, and NMI, then combines it with recall into a pseudo-F1. This aggregation lacks clear theoretical justification and makes it difficult to interpret practical gains.

The proposed supervised contrastive loss appears to be incorrectly formulated: the denominator excludes positives and may even exclude the anchor itself, differing from standard supervised contrastive learning. This raises concerns about whether the method described matches the method implemented.

The adaptive expansion thresholding rule is heuristic and weakly justified. Using average intra-support cosine distance scaled by a global factor may be unstable across attributes with heterogeneous seed diversity.

The candidate generation stage depends heavily on POS patterns extracted from product profiles, which may leak domain-specific structure from external retailer metadata into the task and may limit generalization beyond English or beyond categories with similar profile conventions.
The empirical scope is limited to only four product categories from a single marketplace, so claims about general open-world attribute mining may be overstated.
The paper acknowledges topic collapse in the latent attribute module but does not address it, which weakens confidence in the robustness and necessity of that component.
The span extraction quality remains low, suggesting that much of the overall performance may still be bottlenecked by candidate generation rather than true open-world semantic discovery.

Comparison to stronger modern baselines is limited. The paper mainly compares against OA-Mine and older tagging systems, but not against more recent span-based retrieval, metric learning, or instruction-tuned LLM baselines that could be relevant for open-world extraction.
methodological_flaws: The supervised contrastive objective in Eq. for L_su is mathematically inconsistent with standard supervised contrastive learning. The denominator sums only over negatives N^s(i)=I^s\P^s(i), rather than over all non-anchor examples including positives. This changes the objective substantially and may make the claimed connection to in-batch supervised contrastive learning inaccurate. If the implementation follows the equation, the method is nonstandard; if not, the paper mis-specifies the core loss.

The self-supervised contrastive loss L_ss repeats the same issue: the denominator uses only negatives from different bullet points, not all alternatives. This again departs from standard InfoNCE-style formulations and weakens the scientific clarity of the method.

The latent-variable formulation is not fully rigorous. Eq. (4) samples from N(mu_k^p, sigma_k^p), but variance vs. standard deviation notation is conflated, and positivity constraints on sigma are not specified. The KL term in Eq. (8) is written as KL(tilde alpha^p || hat alpha), although tilde alpha^p is sampled pre-softmax Gaussian variables while hat alpha is described as the prior Product-to-Attribute distribution; the notation mixes Gaussian latent variables with simplex-valued distributions, making the probabilistic model unclear.

The reconstruction objective uses only observed candidate spans in V(p) without any explicit normalization for document length or negative sampling discussion. Since beta is batch-local over unique candidates C, the likelihood is dependent on batch composition, which may introduce instability and makes the probabilistic interpretation approximate at best.

The main evaluation metric is scientifically weak. Averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI into a 'pseudo precision' and then computing pseudo-F1 with recall is ad hoc and not a standard or validated measure for clustering-plus-extraction tasks. Conclusions based primarily on this metric should therefore be treated cautiously.

The test annotation protocol forces each span to have a single attribute type and disallows overlapping spans. For product attributes, this may systematically simplify or distort the task, especially for compositional phrases or values that plausibly belong to multiple attributes. This affects empirical validity of the benchmark.

The seed set and POS patterns are both derived from retailer-provided product profiles, while evaluation is on related product descriptions from the same domain. This creates a risk that the method benefits from structured metadata artifacts not available in truly open-world settings, limiting external validity.
